vignette:
She is fifty-eight now, a rabbi in a coastal congregation, known to others for her calm voice, her careful listening, and the way she seems able to sit beside grief without rushing it away. When she first begins telling her own story, she does so almost apologetically, as if she is more accustomed to holding other people’s fear than naming her own.

The accident happens three years earlier, on a wet winter evening after she has finished visiting a congregant in the hospital. She is driving home on a narrow road outside town, tired but alert, still thinking about the prayer she has just said at a bedside. A truck comes around a bend too fast, skids across the center line, and is suddenly in front of her. She remembers the headlights first, impossibly bright and near, then the violent sound of metal folding into itself. In the instant before impact, she is certain she is about to die. Later, she will say that time does something strange in that moment: everything slows, and one thought flashes through her mind with total clarity—she has not yet called her daughter back.

She survives with broken ribs, a shattered wrist, and a concussion. Trapped in the car, smelling gasoline and rain, she cannot move her legs at first and believes the vehicle might catch fire. She hears someone shouting from far away, though she cannot make out the words. She tries to say the Shema under her breath, but her mouth is full of blood and panic. In the ambulance she drifts in and out, waking each time with the same jolt of terror, as if the crash is still happening.

Her body heals more quickly than the rest of her. In the hospital she startles whenever the intercom crackles. The squeak of a gurney wheel makes her heart race. At night she is back inside the car: the headlights, the crushing sound, the certainty of death. She wakes drenched in sweat, clutching at the blanket as if it were a seatbelt. Friends from the synagogue visit with flowers and casseroles and earnest gratitude that she has been spared. She smiles for them, but inside she feels bewildered and ashamed. She has spent decades helping others make meaning from catastrophe. Now every well-meant phrase about blessing or survival lands on her like pressure.

When she returns home, she assumes normal life will reassemble itself. Instead, her world becomes smaller. She cannot drive past the stretch of road where the accident occurs. At first she tells herself she is being sensible, taking alternate routes while her wrist is still weak. Months later she is adding forty minutes to simple errands to avoid that bend. If rain begins while she is out, her chest tightens so quickly that she has to pull over and call someone to talk her through breathing. She stops visiting congregants in the hospital unless another staff member can drive. She rearranges her rabbinic duties quietly, embarrassed by how much planning it now takes to leave the building.

In services, she finds herself scanning constantly. A latecomer dropping a prayer book can make her jump so hard she loses her place. During pastoral meetings, if someone describes a car accident or sudden death, she feels her skin go cold and her attention slip away. She nods and asks thoughtful questions, but afterward she often realizes she remembers almost nothing of what was said. She begins to dread funerals, not because of the mourners’ pain but because of the procession of cars, the slick roads, the sense of exposure. Before each one, she feels nauseated.

Sleep becomes its own battleground. She avoids going to bed, staying up in the kitchen with tea gone cold beside her, reading sermons she is too tired to edit. She tells herself she is working, but really she is postponing the dreams. On the nights she does sleep, she thrashes awake at 3 a.m., heart pounding, already listening for impact. In the morning she is irritable and brittle. She startles at her phone ringing. She snaps at colleagues, then feels guilty and overcompensates by taking on more than she can manage.

Her daughter tells her she seems far away. Her ex-husband, one of the few people who knew her before ordination, says she has become “all edges.” She hates hearing that, partly because it is true. She no longer trusts the world to stay ordinary. At red lights she grips the wheel until her hands ache. If a car approaches too fast from behind, she is flooded with certainty that she will be hit again. Her mind fills with images she does not want: glass exploding inward, her body pinned, rain on the windshield. She knows she is on a city street in broad daylight, yet her body reacts as if danger is immediate.

What troubles her most is the change in her sense of herself. She has always believed that fear could be met, named, blessed even. Now she feels colonized by it. Standing at the bimah, chanting words she has loved since childhood, she sometimes has the strange sensation that she is performing steadiness rather than inhabiting it. She speaks to others about refuge, remembrance, and the endurance of the soul, while privately counting exits and checking the weather radar. She does not doubt her faith so much as feel estranged from the version of herself who once moved through the world with trust.

By the time she speaks openly about the accident, she is exhausted from the effort of hiding how much of her day is organized around not feeling what still rushes in anyway. She can describe the crash in precise fragments—the headlights, the smell of gasoline, the prayer caught in her throat—but what seems to pain her most is how present it remains. For her, the accident is not over in the way other people imagine. It keeps happening in her sleep, on wet roads, in the sudden clang of dropped metal, in the split second before she turns the ignition key.
